check.x: Professionalism
Hand hygiene, clear introduction, confirms the identity of the parent and baby.
Non-judgemental, empathic approach throughout, including to the vitamin K decision. Acknowledges the parent's worry and guilt without blame.
Uses plain language, checks understanding, invites questions, summarises the plan and confirms Alex agrees.
History
Establishes prolonged jaundice: onset on day 3, persistence beyond 14 days, worse in the last week.
Asks about stool and urine colour:

kids.x: Pale or putty-coloured stools, and asks to see the photo or uses a stool colour chart.

check.x: Asks about bleeding, including the cord stump:

kids.x: Cord stump bleeding: timing and how long it took to stop.
Bruising, nosebleeds, bleeding from other sites, blood in vomit or nappy.

check.x: Asks whether vitamin K was given at birth (injection or oral) and why it was declined, using open, non-blaming questions.
Screens for red flags: feeding, wet nappies, weight gain, vomiting, drowsiness or irritability, fever, fits.
Asks relevant birth, antenatal and family history:

kids.x: Antenatal scan findings, including the two-vessel cord, gestation, mode of birth, presentation and birth weight.
Family history of liver disease and bleeding disorders, and of hip dysplasia in first-degree relatives.

check.x: Asks briefly how and where Noah sleeps and about smoke exposure.
Explores Alex's ideas, concerns and expectations, including the breastmilk jaundice and sunshine ideas.
Examination
General inspection: alertness, tone and cry, extent of the jaundice and scleral icterus, pallor.
Examines the abdomen for the liver and spleen (firm liver edge 2 cm below the costal margin, spleen not palpable).
Inspects the stool and urine in the nappy (or the photo) against a stool colour chart.
Looks for bleeding: umbilicus (separated, dry, not bleeding), bruising, petechiae and the heel-prick sites.
Checks hydration and growth: fontanelle, mucous membranes, weight against birth weight; listens to the heart and feels the femoral pulses.
Examines the hips: Barlow and Ortolani, symmetry of abduction, leg lengths and skin creases.
Interpretation
Recognises jaundice beyond 14 days in a term baby with pale stools, dark urine and a firm liver as cholestasis until proven otherwise, and says biliary atresia must be urgently excluded.

Recognises the cord-stump bleed in an infant who had no vitamin K prophylaxis and who has cholestasis as a possible warning bleed of late vitamin K deficiency bleeding (VKDB), with the risk of bleeding in the brain.
Explains why this is not breastmilk jaundice: breastmilk jaundice is unconjugated with normal yellow stools, while pale stools and dark urine point to conjugated (cholestatic) jaundice.
Interprets the observations and growth: well, thriving, normal BGL, and states that a well, thriving baby does not exclude biliary atresia.
Interprets the stool colour chart: pale colours in the abnormal range, confirming acholic stools.

Interprets the records: an isolated single umbilical artery with a normal renal tract and heart on the morphology scan, a normal newborn examination including hips, and vitamin K not recorded (so the history is what confirms it was declined).
Management

Arranges same-day urgent paediatric or ED assessment regardless of pending results. Does not make referral conditional on a split bilirubin result and does not send the baby for outpatient bloods and wait:

kids.x: Phones the paediatric registrar or ED ahead and gives a verbal handover.
Provides a written referral stating age, jaundice duration, pale stools, dark urine, no vitamin K, the cord bleed and the two-vessel cord.
Arranges safe direct transfer (ambulance or accompanied by the parent) without delay.

check.x: Ensures urgent coagulation studies (PT/INR) are done with the cholestasis work-up:

kids.x: Split (total and conjugated) bilirubin, liver function tests, full blood count.
States vitamin K treatment must not wait for the results.

check.x: Recommends vitamin K 1 mg by injection (the fixed dose for a term baby) without waiting for results or delaying transfer, and does not accept oral vitamin K as an alternative: IV by the receiving team is preferred to treat suspected deficiency, or IM by the GP before transfer if the receiving team advises it:

kids.x: Blood may be taken for coagulation studies first only if this causes no delay.
Explains oral vitamin K is not suitable here: cholestasis impairs absorption of fat-soluble vitamins, oral dosing is less reliable, and active deficiency is possible.
Does not offer the oral option as a parental choice.

check.x: Respects the parent's autonomy while clearly recommending vitamin K by injection. If the parent declines, explains the risks again, involves the paediatric consultant urgently, documents the informed refusal and still sends Noah to hospital today.
Gives the urgent plan first and keeps the hip, cord and sleep counselling brief.
Explains vitamin K in plain language and corrects the vaccine misconception:

kids.x: It is not a vaccine. It is a vitamin that helps blood clot, and newborns are born with low levels.
Without it, rare but serious bleeding can occur, including in the brain, for up to six months, and a single injection works best.

check.x: Explains the likely problem and its urgency in plain language:

kids.x: Pale stools and dark urine suggest bile is not draining properly from the liver; if biliary atresia is the cause, early surgery (Kasai procedure, ideally before about 8 weeks of age) gives the best outcome.
The jaundice is not caused by declining vitamin K, but the lack of vitamin K adds a bleeding risk.
Advises against sunlight as treatment: it does not help this type of jaundice and is unsafe for a newborn.

check.x: Two-vessel cord (brief): often a normal variant with a slightly higher chance of an undetected kidney or heart anomaly. The morphology scan and newborn heart examination were normal, so Noah will have a renal tract ultrasound, with cardiac assessment only if the heart examination is abnormal or an anomaly is suspected. Does not imply an echocardiogram is needed for every isolated two-vessel cord.

Hips (brief): Noah's hips are normal on Barlow (can a located hip be pushed out) and Ortolani (does a dislocated hip clunk back in). Alex's sister's baby is Noah's cousin, not a first-degree relative, so this is not a standard risk factor, and the plan is hip checks at routine visits, not a routine hip ultrasound.

Explains SUDI and SIDS: SUDI is the umbrella term for sudden unexpected death in infancy, including SIDS and fatal sleep accidents; SIDS is the sudden unexpected death of a baby under 1 year, usually during sleep, with no cause found after full investigation.

Gives safe sleep advice (at least four measures) and corrects the unsafe practices described: on the back with feet at the foot of the cot, never on the tummy; head and face uncovered with no pillows, toys or loose bedding and no sofa sleeping; a cot meeting Australian standards with a firm flat mattress and lightweight tucked-in bedding or a light wrap that leaves the hips and legs free to bend, not a fluffy blanket; smoke-free environment; own safe sleep space in the same room as a caregiver for the first 6 to 12 months; continue breastfeeding.
Safety netting
Tells Alex to call 000 if Noah bleeds, becomes drowsy or floppy, vomits, has a fit or a bulging soft spot on the way to hospital or while waiting, and to keep breastfeeding.
Tells Alex to go straight to the hospital today, not home first, and that the team is expecting them.

Offers written information (Red Nose safe sleeping, stool colour chart, hospital information) and arranges follow-up: GP review after discharge, hip checks at routine visits, renal tract ultrasound. Documents the vitamin K discussion.

desc: This station involves a focused history from the parent and a focused examination of an 18-day-old with prolonged jaundice, pale stools and an earlier cord-stump bleed after vitamin K was declined, then interpreting the observations, stool colour chart and antenatal and newborn records, arranging same-day urgent assessment with vitamin K by injection, and briefly counselling on the two-vessel cord, hips and safe sleep.
explain:
Cholestasis until proven otherwise

Jaundice beyond 14 days in a term baby needs a split (total and conjugated) bilirubin. Pale putty stools, dark urine and a firm liver make cholestasis likely, and biliary atresia must be urgently excluded. Breastmilk jaundice is unconjugated, the stools stay yellow and the baby is well; it does not explain pale stools. A well, thriving baby with normal observations does not exclude biliary atresia. Outcomes after Kasai portoenterostomy are best when surgery is done early, ideally before about 8 weeks of age. A GP cannot order a test and wait: Noah needs same-day paediatric or ED assessment whatever the pending results.

Interpreting the Part 2 results

The stool colour chart match at the pale end confirms acholic stools. The observations, BGL and weight gain show a stable baby who can travel with a parent, but they change nothing about the urgency. The morphology scan shows an isolated single umbilical artery with a normal renal tract and heart. The discharge summary records a normal newborn examination including hips, and does not record vitamin K, so the history is what tells you it was declined.

The cord bleed and vitamin K deficiency bleeding

Vitamin K is a vitamin that helps blood clot. It is not a vaccine, and newborns are born with low levels. Late VKDB occurs from about 2 to 12 weeks and can occur up to 6 months, with intracranial haemorrhage a major risk. Risk factors include no prophylaxis, exclusive breastfeeding and cholestasis. A cord-stump bleed that was slow to stop in an unprophylaxed, now cholestatic infant may be a warning bleed. The plan is urgent coagulation studies (PT/INR) and vitamin K 1 mg by injection straight away, without waiting for the results. To treat suspected deficiency it is usually given by slow IV injection in hospital, which works quickly and avoids a haematoma from an IM injection if clotting is already deranged; if the receiving team asks the GP to give it before transfer, IM is the route available.

Why oral vitamin K is not an option here

Oral prophylaxis needs several doses and protects less reliably. Cholestasis impairs absorption of fat-soluble vitamins, and active deficiency may already be present. Clinicians should clearly recommend treatment by injection while respecting the parent's autonomy. If the parent declines, explain the risks again, involve the paediatric consultant urgently and document the informed refusal. Do not accept oral drops as a compromise.

Sunlight and jaundice

Sunlight is not a treatment for cholestatic jaundice and is unsafe for newborns because of the risk of sunburn. Phototherapy treats unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia and does not address this problem.

Two-vessel cord

A two-vessel cord (single umbilical artery) can be a normal variant, but it raises the chance of an undetected congenital anomaly, especially of the renal tract and the heart. For an isolated finding with a normal antenatal scan and normal newborn examination, renal tract ultrasound is commonly arranged. Cardiac assessment (echocardiogram) is indicated if an anomaly is suspected or the newborn examination is abnormal, not automatically for every isolated two-vessel cord.

Hips

Barlow tests whether a located hip can be dislocated (adduct the flexed hip with gentle backward pressure). Ortolani relocates a dislocated hip (abduct the flexed hip while lifting the greater trochanter forward), felt as a clunk. A positive or abnormal finding needs hip ultrasound and paediatric or orthopaedic review. Noah's cousin (Alex's sister's baby) is not a first-degree relative, so the cousin's DDH is not a standard risk factor. Tight wrapping with the legs held straight is itself a risk for hip dysplasia, so any wrap should leave the hips and legs free to bend. With a normal documented hip examination and no first-degree family history, the plan is continued hip checks at routine visits, with ultrasound only if the examination is abnormal or other risk factors (for example first-degree family history or breech presentation) are present.

SUDI, SIDS and safe sleep

SUDI is the umbrella term for sudden unexpected death in infancy and includes SIDS and fatal sleep accidents such as accidental suffocation. SIDS is the sudden unexpected death of a baby under 1 year, usually during sleep, with no cause found after thorough investigation. Risk reduction: sleep on the back with feet at the foot of the cot, face and head uncovered with nothing loose near the head, a cot meeting Australian standards with a firm flat mattress and lightweight tucked-in bedding, a smoke-free environment, the baby's own safe sleep space in the same room as a caregiver for the first 6 to 12 months, and breastfeeding if possible. Sofa sleeping, pillows and tummy sleeping are particular hazards.

Prioritising and safety netting

With a baby who may have both cholestasis and an active vitamin K deficiency, the urgent referral comes first. Hip, cord and sleep counselling can be brief, with written resources and follow-up for the rest. On the way to hospital, bleeding, drowsiness, floppiness, vomiting, a fit or a bulging fontanelle (possible intracranial bleeding) mean calling 000.
focus: Newborn check and parent counselling: vitamin K, hips, jaundice, safe sleep
guide:
In Part 1 the examiner gives findings from the Exam findings only when the candidate says what they would examine. Alex raises the vitamin K, sunshine, hip and SUDI questions during Part 1; brief answers then, or a promise to come back to them, are fine, and the counselling items are marked whenever they are covered, in Part 1 or Part 2. In Part 2 the examiner hands over the results and puts Alex's remaining questions (a lab test and waiting, vitamin K drops, the two-vessel cord).

A high-performing candidate finds the pale stools, dark urine and the cord-stump bleed, asks about vitamin K without blame, and finds the firm liver on examination. They recognise cholestasis until proven otherwise, so biliary atresia must be excluded urgently, and a possible warning bleed of late VKDB. They arrange same-day paediatric or ED assessment by phone and letter without waiting for any result, ensure PT/INR is done with the split bilirubin, and recommend vitamin K by injection now, explaining why drops are not acceptable here. They respect Alex's autonomy and escalate if Alex declines. Once the urgent plan is set, they answer the cord, hip and sleep questions briefly and give specific red flags.

A borderline candidate notes the jaundice but does not link the pale stools, dark urine and cord bleed. They may order a split bilirubin and wait, offer oral vitamin K drops as a choice, order a hip ultrasound because of the sister's baby, imply an echocardiogram is mandatory for the two-vessel cord, spend most of the time on hips and sleep, or sound judgemental about the vitamin K decision.
patient:
Role: You are Alex Nguyen, parent of Noah, who is 18 days old and your first baby. You are tired, anxious and a little defensive about the vitamin K decision. You become tearful if blamed. Noah is with you and the examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings when the candidate says what they would examine.

Opening line: "Noah is still really yellow. My mum says it's just breastmilk jaundice."

History (give only when asked):

  • Jaundice: noticed on day 3. It improved a little but never went away, and he has looked more yellow in the last week.
  • Stools: mustard yellow at first. Since about day 10 they have been getting paler. Now they are pale grey-white, like putty. You have a photo on your phone and show it if asked.
  • Urine: the nappies are dark yellow-brown and stain.
  • Feeding and general: breastfed about 8 times a day with a good latch, plenty of wet nappies. He wakes for feeds and is not floppy or drowsy. No vomiting, fever, fits or unusual irritability. No falls or knocks to the head that you know of.
  • Bleeding: around day 9 the cord stump bled as it was about to fall off. It soaked a cloth and you pressed on it for 10 to 15 minutes before it stopped. The midwife said it was probably normal. No bruises, nosebleeds, bleeding from the mouth, blood in vomit or blood in the nappy. Nothing is bleeding today.
  • Vitamin K (say this only when asked about vitamin K or injections): "We said no to it at the hospital. We thought it was a vaccine and we're not comfortable with vaccines. He had no drops either." You signed a form.
  • Pregnancy and birth: uncomplicated pregnancy, antenatal blood tests normal as far as you know. The 20-week scan said the cord has two vessels instead of three, and nobody has mentioned it since. No diabetes, medicines, alcohol or drugs. Born at 39 weeks by normal vaginal birth, head first, weighing 3.4 kg. Home on day 2. The heel-prick test was done.
  • Family: no family history of liver disease, bleeding disorders or jaundice in babies. You and your partner are not related. Your sister's baby needed a hip brace. Neither you nor your partner had hip problems as babies.
  • Medicines and allergies: none for Noah. You take no medicines.
  • Sleep and home (only if asked): Noah sleeps in your bed, or on the couch on a pillow with you when you are exhausted. He is wrapped tightly in a fluffy blanket and is sometimes put on his tummy because he settles. Your partner smokes on the balcony. Your mum helps most days.

Ideas, concerns, expectations: you think it is breastmilk jaundice, as your mum says, and wonder if he just needs more sun. You are worried it is your fault for saying no to vitamin K. You expect a blood test at the lab and to be told it will settle.

Questions to raise in Part 1 (one at a time):

  • When vitamin K comes up: "Is it because we said no to vitamin K? Did we cause this?"
  • During the history: "Do we just need more sunshine?" Accept the answer if the candidate advises against it and explains why. If told sunlight is fine, say "OK, I'll take him to the park."
  • When the candidate examines the hips: "My sister's baby needed a hip brace. Should Noah have a hip scan?"
  • If the candidate asks about sleep, or near the end of Part 1: "A friend's baby died last year and they said SUDI, not SIDS. Is that different?"

In Part 2 the examiner puts your remaining questions (waiting for a lab test, vitamin K drops, the two-vessel cord) to the candidate. Interrupt if the candidate uses medical jargon without explaining it.
points: Jaundice beyond 14 days in a term baby, especially with pale stools and dark urine, is cholestasis until proven otherwise. Refer for same-day paediatric or ED assessment, not outpatient tests.
A cord bleed in an infant who had no vitamin K and has cholestasis may be a warning bleed of late VKDB. Get urgent PT/INR and give vitamin K 1 mg by injection (IV in hospital) without delay.
Vitamin K is not a vaccine. Oral vitamin K is not an acceptable alternative in cholestasis or suspected VKDB, so recommend the injection clearly and escalate if the parent declines.
Sunlight is not a treatment for jaundice in newborns.
A two-vessel cord is often a normal variant: arrange renal tract ultrasound, with cardiac review only if an anomaly is suspected or the examination is abnormal.
A normal hip examination with DDH only in a cousin means routine hip checks. Order ultrasound only for an abnormal examination or true risk factors (first-degree family history, breech).

stem: You are a GP. Alex Nguyen has brought in Noah, their 18-day-old son, because "he is still yellow". A tertiary children's hospital with a paediatric emergency department is about half an hour away by car. A practice nurse is available to help.
tasks: Take a focused history from Alex and perform a focused examination of Noah, telling the examiner what you are examining and why (10 minutes).

The examiner will give you Noah's observations, a stool colour chart comparison, his 20-week morphology scan report and his hospital discharge summary. Interpret them, then outline your management approach for today, answer Alex's questions about vitamin K, the two-vessel cord, hips and safe sleep briefly, and give your safety netting (5 minutes).
title: Pale stools and a bleeding cord stump in a jaundiced 18-day-old

part2.lead: Here are Noah's observations from the practice nurse, the stool colour chart comparison, his 20-week morphology scan report and his day 2 hospital discharge summary.

handover.label: Observations
handover.result: HR 140, RR 40, temperature 36.8 °C, SpO2 98% on room air, CRT under 2 seconds, BGL 4.3 mmol/L. Weight 3.7 kg (birth weight 3.4 kg), gaining appropriately.

handover.label: Stool colour chart
handover.result: Today's nappy and the photo on Alex's phone both match the palest cards on the infant stool colour chart (pale grey-white, the abnormal range). Urine in the nappy dark yellow-brown and staining.

handover.label: 20-week morphology ultrasound report
handover.result: Single umbilical artery (two-vessel cord). Fetal kidneys and bladder normal. Four-chamber view and outflow tracts of the heart normal. Growth on the 50th centile. No other structural anomaly seen.

handover.label: Hospital discharge summary (day 2)
handover.result: Term (39+3 weeks) spontaneous vaginal birth, cephalic. Birth weight 3.4 kg. Two-vessel umbilical cord noted at birth. Newborn examination normal, including hips (Barlow and Ortolani negative) and heart sounds. Newborn bloodspot screening collected. Vitamin K: not recorded.

ask: What do these results and your examination findings show?
What is the most likely problem, and what else worries you about Noah today?
What is your management today? Alex asks: "Can we get the blood test at the lab and come back tomorrow? And could he have vitamin K drops instead of the injection?"
Briefly, what do you tell Alex about the two-vessel cord, a hip scan and safe sleep?
What safety netting and follow-up do you arrange?
